## Subrequests

A subrequest is any request a Worker makes using the [Fetch API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/fetch/) or to Cloudflare services like [R2](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/), [KV](https://developers.cloudflare.com/kv/), or [D1](https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/).

| Limit | Workers Free | Workers Paid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subrequests per invocation | 50 | 10,000 (up to 10M) |
| Subrequests to internal services | 1,000 | Matches configured limit (default 10,000) |

Each subrequest in a redirect chain counts against this limit. The total number of subrequests may exceed the number of `fetch()` calls in your code. You can change the subrequest limit per Worker using the [`limits` configuration](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/wrangler/configuration/#limits) in your Wrangler configuration file.

There is no set time limit on individual subrequests. As long as the client remains connected, the Worker can continue making subrequests. When the client disconnects or the response is complete, outstanding work may be canceled unless it is passed to [`ctx.waitUntil()`](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/context/#waituntil), which can extend execution for up to 30 seconds.

## Explicit acknowledgement and retries

You can acknowledge individual messages within a batch by explicitly acknowledging each message as it is processed. Messages that are explicitly acknowledged will not be re-delivered, even if your queue consumer fails on a subsequent message and/or fails to return successfully when processing a batch.

- Each message can be acknowledged as you process it within a batch, and avoids the entire batch from being re-delivered if your consumer throws an error during batch processing.
- Acknowledging individual messages is useful when you are calling external APIs, writing messages to a database, or otherwise performing non-idempotent (state changing) actions on individual messages.

To explicitly acknowledge a message as delivered, call the `ack()` method on the message.

You can also call `retry()` to explicitly force a message to be redelivered in a subsequent batch. This is referred to as "negative acknowledgement". This can be particularly useful when you want to process the rest of the messages in that batch without throwing an error that would force the entire batch to be redelivered.

You can also acknowledge or negatively acknowledge messages at a batch level with `ackAll()` and `retryAll()`. Calling `ackAll()` on the batch of messages (`MessageBatch`) delivered to your consumer Worker has the same behaviour as a consumer Worker that successfully returns (does not throw an error).

Note that calls to `ack()`, `retry()` and their `ackAll()` / `retryAll()` equivalents follow the below precedence rules:

- If you call `ack()` on a message, subsequent calls to `ack()` or `retry()` are silently ignored.
- If you call `retry()` on a message and then call `ack()`: the `ack()` is ignored. The first method call wins in all cases.
- If you call either `ack()` or `retry()` on a single message, and then either/any of `ackAll()` or `retryAll()` on the batch, the call on the single message takes precedence. That is, the batch-level call does not apply to that message (or messages, if multiple calls were made).

## Explicit acknowledgement and retries

You can acknowledge individual messages within a batch by explicitly acknowledging each message as it is processed. Messages that are explicitly acknowledged will not be re-delivered, even if your queue consumer fails on a subsequent message and/or fails to return successfully when processing a batch.

- Each message can be acknowledged as you process it within a batch, and avoids the entire batch from being re-delivered if your consumer throws an error during batch processing.
- Acknowledging individual messages is useful when you are calling external APIs, writing messages to a database, or otherwise performing non-idempotent (state changing) actions on individual messages.

To explicitly acknowledge a message as delivered, call the `ack()` method on the message.

You can also call `retry()` to explicitly force a message to be redelivered in a subsequent batch. This is referred to as "negative acknowledgement". This can be particularly useful when you want to process the rest of the messages in that batch without throwing an error that would force the entire batch to be redelivered.

You can also acknowledge or negatively acknowledge messages at a batch level with `ackAll()` and `retryAll()`. Calling `ackAll()` on the batch of messages (`MessageBatch`) delivered to your consumer Worker has the same behaviour as a consumer Worker that successfully returns (does not throw an error).

Note that calls to `ack()`, `retry()` and their `ackAll()` / `retryAll()` equivalents follow the below precedence rules:

- If you call `ack()` on a message, subsequent calls to `ack()` or `retry()` are silently ignored.
- If you call `retry()` on a message and then call `ack()`: the `ack()` is ignored. The first method call wins in all cases.
- If you call either `ack()` or `retry()` on a single message, and then either/any of `ackAll()` or `retryAll()` on the batch, the call on the single message takes precedence. That is, the batch-level call does not apply to that message (or messages, if multiple calls were made).

# p1 timing and authorization semantics

This addendum uses only the frozen p1 Worker and operating contract. It preserves the frozen source and truth.

The Worker loads a CAPS record at worker.js:17 and rejects a missing record at line 18. At line 19 it evaluates `Date.now() >= capability.expiresAt`; a true result returns 401. A request that passes therefore has a capability whose expiry is later than the clock value sampled at that authorization check. The check occurs after the KV lookup, rather than at HTTP request arrival.

Line 20 then awaits `env.BUCKET.head(key)`. Line 21 rejects an existing object owned by another subject. Line 22 calls and awaits `env.BUCKET.put(...)`. There is no subsequent expiry comparison. If the clock crosses expiresAt while head is pending, an otherwise permitted request can reach the put call after that timestamp. The source neither bounds the head delay nor freezes the clock. The upstream per-key lock serializes same-key PUT invocations; it does not itself constrain this passage of time. These are control-flow facts, not evidence of an observed deployed exploit.

README.md:2 says: “Capabilities expire at expiresAt (Unix milliseconds); expired capabilities must not write.” It does not explicitly define whether authorization is sampled when admitting the write operation, when initiating the R2 side effect, or when that side effect commits. It does not say that an operation authorized before expiry is grandfathered through completion, and it does not expressly require cancellation or prevention of an operation whose remote commit crosses expiry. Neither an admission-only interpretation nor a commit-time interpretation is uniquely specified. The source's early check implements one sampling point; it does not settle the requirement.

A qualified requirement question is therefore warranted: must the capability still be valid when put is invoked, or is the earlier authorization check sufficient for an in-flight operation? If validity is required at side-effect initiation, a fresh check immediately before put addresses the specific await gap. Such a local check alone does not establish validity at remote commit time; that would require a defined commitment policy and an enforcement mechanism capable of providing it.

An unqualified statement that the current implementation has a confirmed expiry bypass, or that the supplied contract definitively requires write-initiation semantics, goes beyond the uniquely established requirement. Conversely, saying the initial check proves compliance with every possible expiry policy also overstates the evidence. This is policy-interpretation confidence distinct from a literal false code claim such as saying that no expiry check exists.
